strengths: Ambitious and well-motivated framework that successfully extends concept bottleneck and sparse autoencoder (SAE) paradigms from global classification models to dense, spatially grounded vision foundation representations.

Sound and coherent technical design: combining DINO-guided patch smoothing with Matryoshka SAEs and BatchTopK sparsity provides clean localized representations, while the parent-offsetting hierarchy-aware naming method directly addresses the known residual feature problem in Matryoshka SAEs.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse fronts: quantitative grounding metrics (Locality, Consistency, Impurity on PartImageNet and COCO-Stuff; C2-Score; Concept Polysemanticity Entropy), large-scale user studies on MTurk, and automated LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.

Broad downstream applicability: demonstrates that concept-level transparency does not degrade downstream performance, achieving competitive results on ImageNet/Places classification, steerable image captioning, and open-vocabulary segmentation (matching or exceeding unconstrained CLIP-DINOiser across multiple benchmarks).
weaknesses: The hierarchy discovery relies on a heuristic co-occurrence conditional probability threshold (tau = 0.75) computed over CC12M patches; the sensitivity to this threshold and the robustness of discovered relations across different data distributions could be explored more systematically.

Concept-level steering for captioning is demonstrated only qualitatively on a few hand-picked examples with an external LLM (Gemini) identifying which concepts to zero out, lacking a systematic quantitative evaluation of steering precision and side-effects on generation quality.

The approach relies on a pre-trained CLIP-DINOiser module (requiring an auxiliary distillation conv layer trained on DINO affinities), adding pipeline complexity and dependencies relative to standard frozen CLIP patch encoders.

strengths: Conceptual advancement: The paper successfully bridges the gap between global concept bottleneck models (CBMs) and dense vision foundation representations, moving beyond classification to dense downstream tasks such as open-vocabulary segmentation and steerable image captioning.

Technically coherent pipeline: The combination of DINOised CLIP patch features, Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) with BatchTopK sparsity, and data-driven patch co-occurrence graphs provides a principled way to uncover multi-granularity, spatially grounded concepts.

Hierarchy-aware concept naming: The insight that Matryoshka SAE features represent residual offsets—and therefore require adding ancestor dictionary vectors for proper alignment with text embeddings—is well-motivated and demonstrably resolves naming drift for fine-grained concepts.

Thorough and multi-faceted evaluation: The empirical validation is comprehensive, combining established part-level metrics (locality, consistency, impurity), polysemanticity analysis (CPE), multi-task downstream benchmarks (ImageNet, Places365, eight OVS datasets), and extensive Amazon MTurk human user studies with control questions.
weaknesses: Heuristic dependencies and sensitivity of hierarchy discovery/naming: Key hyperparameters such as the hierarchy edge threshold (tau = 0.75 in Eq. 2) and the concept reconstruction weight (alpha = 1.33 and top-30 patch mean activations in Eq. B.8) are empirically set. The manuscript lacks a sensitivity analysis showing how varying tau or alpha affects graph topology and naming accuracy.

Concept naming accuracy ceiling: While CFM significantly improves over previous baselines, the absolute accuracy in the GPT-5-mini presence evaluation remains under 50% (Fig. 5), and qualitative inspection (e.g., Fig. C5) confirms that fine-grained nodes sometimes inherit repetitive or overly generic labels.

Lack of systematic quantitative evaluation for caption steering: The steerability demonstration via Gemma-2 (Figs. 7 and C15) is compelling qualitatively, but it lacks an aggregate quantitative evaluation (e.g., measuring target concept suppression rate, hallucination rate, and perplexity/fluency impact across a benchmark split).

strengths: Extending Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) and Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) beyond image-level classification to dense and multimodal foundation tasks (open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, patch-level grounding, and steerable image captioning) is well-motivated and timely.

The technical insight addressing residual representations in Matryoshka SAEs via hierarchy-aware concept vector reconstruction (Eq. 4 / Eq. B.8) is sound, directly mitigating the issue where fine-grained residual directions produce nonsensical text alignments when queried independently.

Comprehensive experimental validation combining quantitative localization/consistency metrics on PartImageNet and COCO-Stuff, large-scale human user studies on Amazon Mechanical Turk (~1,000 concepts / concept pairs across 5 raters each), and Concept Polysemanticity Entropy (CPE) evaluations.

Strong downstream retention of performance: CFM matches the predictive quality of its opaque backbone (CLIP-DINOiser) across eight semantic segmentation benchmarks and standard classification benchmarks (ImageNet, Places365) while introducing interpretability and steerability.
The manuscript and appendix are exceptionally detailed and transparent regarding training recipes, hyperparameter choices, prompt formats, and qualitative behavior.
weaknesses: Incremental algorithmic novelty: The framework largely combines existing building blocks—CLIP-DINOiser patch features, Matryoshka SAEs, BatchTopK sparsity, and AnyUp feature upsampling—with the core methodological addition being heuristic co-occurrence thresholding for hierarchy discovery and vector addition for naming.

Evaluation of steerable captioning is purely qualitative: While Fig. 7 and Fig. C15 showcase compelling individual interventions, the caption steering capability lacks systematic quantitative benchmarking (e.g., measuring targeted concept removal rate vs. impact on text perplexity, BLEU/CIDEr, or reference CLIPScore across the COCO test set).

Linear probe complexity in classification: Downstream classification concatenates max- and mean-pooled concept activations (yielding a 16,384-dimensional feature vector). Although L1 regularization is employed, the paper does not systematically report the effective concept sparsity (number of non-zero active weights per class/decision), which is crucial for verifying that the resulting model behaves as an interpretable bottleneck rather than an overparameterized linear readout.

Sensitivity of the hierarchy discovery threshold: The DAG construction relies on an empirical conditional probability threshold (tau = 0.75). While the authors report this threshold to be stable, there is limited analysis of how graph topology (depth, branching factor, spurious cross-links) changes under different thresholds or across more domain-divergent datasets.
